documents.title: XVA market and counterparty data documentation

sections.heading: Purpose and scope
sections.text: This document describes the reference data set of the Derivatives Valuation and XVA model (inventory identifier MDL-14, model version 4.2): the trade, netting, collateral, counterparty and market data used to calculate the credit valuation adjustment (CVA), debit valuation adjustment (DVA) and funding valuation adjustment (FVA) of the Bank's bilateral OTC derivatives, and the data used to calibrate the exposure simulation. The data set is used for the month-end fair value of the derivatives portfolio under IFRS 13, the daily XVA risk management of the XVA desk and the calculation of the unearned credit spread, investing and funding cost and model risk additional valuation adjustments by Product Control. It follows the RDS documentation template of MRM-STD-021 Annex A; the model was approved before version 3.0 of that standard and its documentation is migrated to the template with this major version, with sections that address credit default data retained as "Not applicable" and justified. The frozen data set referenced throughout is XVA-RDS-2026Q4-F1, which is also referenced in chapter 3 of the XVA methodology document (EVD-14-MDD).

sections.heading: Governance and ownership of data
sections.text: The data are sourced from five data domains, each with one Data Owner in the Group Data Catalogue: Trading Positions and Valuations (Head of Product Control), Market Data (Head of Market Data Services), Legal Agreements and Collateral (Head of Collateral Management), Counterparty Reference Data (Head of Client Data Management) and Funding and Transfer Pricing (Head of Treasury). The model data are mapped to these domains per variable in Annex A. The model owner agreed the data quality expectations for the critical data elements with the five Data Owners in DQA-FOQ-2025-02 of 3 December 2025, reconfirmed on 15 January 2027. Business ownership of risk data lies with the Data Owners and Data Stewards, and IT ownership with the Valuation Platform team, which operates the XVA engine and its data store. Data quality of the model data is managed in accordance with MRM-STD-022, as documented in the data quality report EVD-14-DQ.

sections.heading: Observation period
sections.text: XVA-RDS-2026Q4-F1 contains the portfolio snapshot of 31 December 2026 (16,700 bilateral OTC derivative trades in 2,310 netting sets with 1,452 counterparties), the market data of that date, weekly risk factor returns from 5 January 2024 to 25 December 2026 (156 observations) for the correlation calibration, daily five-year CDS spreads of 1,108 liquid reference entities from 2 January 2025 to 31 December 2026 (511 business days) for the proxy regression, and monthly exposure back-testing anchor dates from January 2019 to December 2026. As the model has no default-based target, the target event count is replaced by the number of back-testing observations: 96 monthly anchor dates with 1,020 realised risk factor paths per horizon. The data set holds 2.9 million records in total, of which 2.1 million are market data observations.

sections.heading: Choice of observation window
sections.text: The three-year window for correlations balances responsiveness and statistical stability; it contains the 2024 easing cycle and the market turbulence of April 2025, and correlations estimated over five years including the 2022 rate shock differ by less than 0.05 for the main pairs (sensitivity in EVD-14-MDD section 7.4). The two-year window for the proxy regression reflects the liquidity of the CDS market; a longer window would include reference entities whose liquidity has since changed. The back-testing window from 2019 covers the negative rate period, the COVID-19 turmoil, the 2022 rate shock and the 2023 banking stress. Volatilities and drifts are not estimated from history: the exposure model is calibrated risk-neutrally to market prices of the valuation date, consistently with the pricing of the trades.

sections.heading: Target variable and outcome horizon
sections.text: The model has no default-based target variable; its outputs are fair value adjustments measured at the valuation date. The outcome variables used for performance testing are (i) realised risk factor moves over horizons of 1 week to 1 year, against which the simulated distributions are back-tested, (ii) the daily XVA P&L explain, and (iii) CDS spreads of liquid reference entities excluded from the proxy regression, against which proxy spreads are tested out of sample. The critical data elements are the trade economics, netting and collateral agreement terms, collateral balances, market data used for calibration, CDS and proxy spreads, recovery rates and the funding curve.

sections.heading: Deviations from the Bank's definition of default
sections.text: Not applicable. The model does not construct default flags from the Bank's obligor data; counterparty default risk enters the CVA through market-implied default probabilities derived from CDS or proxy spreads. Counterparties in default under CR-STD-110 are flagged from the Credit Rating System and excluded from the CVA calculation; their derivative receivables are measured by Product Control with a specific credit adjustment based on the expected recovery, as described in section 4.2.

sections.heading: Default definition
sections.text: Not applicable for the CVA calculation, which uses market-implied default probabilities. The default status of counterparties is taken from the Credit Rating System, which applies the prudential definition of default of CR-STD-110; the market-implied default probabilities refer to the credit events of the ISDA Credit Derivatives Definitions, and the two concepts are labelled distinctly in the Group Data Catalogue (DEF_PRUD and CDS_CREDIT_EVENT) with the difference documented in Annex A. In 2026 three counterparties defaulted, with derivative fair values of EUR 4.1 million before specific adjustments.

sections.heading: Unlikeliness-to-pay triggers
sections.text: Not applicable. The model does not determine default status and therefore does not apply unlikeliness-to-pay triggers. The default status of counterparties is received from the Credit Rating System, where unlikeliness-to-pay triggers are applied by Credit Risk Management under CR-STD-110, and a change in status is reflected in the next daily XVA run. Rating downgrades that do not constitute a default are reflected through the proxy mapping of section 4.1.3 at the next monthly update.

sections.heading: Data sources and lineage
sections.text: The data set draws on the trading system Apex (trades and front-office valuations), the legal agreement database LegalHub (ISDA master agreements, CSAs and netting opinions), the collateral management system CollatPro (collateral balances and margin calls), the Market Data Repository (curves, volatilities, CDS spreads), the counterparty master RefHub and Treasury's funds transfer pricing system (funding curve). An authoritative source is defined for each type of data, and the authoritative sources are recorded in Annex A. Lineage from the source systems to the RDS and to the production input data of the XVA engine is documented for every variable in Annex A, including raw fields used only to derive retained variables, such as CSA threshold currencies used to convert thresholds. For each variable the lineage identifies the source fields, the Valuation Platform staging tables, every transformation, filter, join and aggregation with the ETL job reference (for example xva_ns_build_v3 and csa_terms_map_v2), and the extraction frequency and timing (daily at 19:00 CET). The lineage allows every netting set exposure and every XVA figure to be traced from the source system to the general ledger posting.

sections.heading: Trade, netting and collateral data
sections.text: Trades are extracted from Apex at the 17:30 CET end-of-day snapshot with their economic terms and front-office valuations; netting set membership is derived from LegalHub, where each ISDA master agreement carries the result of the legal netting opinion for the counterparty's jurisdiction. Trades are aggregated by netting set only where an enforceable master netting agreement exists; trades without a positive netting opinion (97 trades at 31 December 2026) are treated as separate netting sets. CSA terms (thresholds, minimum transfer amounts, independent amounts, eligible collateral, margin frequency and dispute terms) are taken from LegalHub, and collateral balances from CollatPro. Trades and collateral cover all legal entities of the Bank that face bilateral derivative counterparties (the Amsterdam head office and the London branch) and all product types.

sections.heading: Market data and credit curves
sections.text: Interest rate curves, swaption and cap volatilities, FX rates and FX option volatilities and inflation swap rates are taken from the Market Data Repository at the official close; they are the same data as used for the front-office valuation of the trades. Single-name CDS spreads and recovery rates are received from S&P Global Market Intelligence; for this third-party data the lineage starts at receipt in the MDR landing zone and records the provider, the data product (S&P Global CDS Pricing End-of-Day) and the delivery date and file version. Model inputs are sourced in line with market prices wherever possible: 96% of the calibration instruments are quoted instruments, and the remaining inputs (long-dated volatilities beyond 30 years and illiquid FX volatilities) are extrapolated with documented methods. The funding curve is received monthly from Treasury's funds transfer pricing system as the spread of the Bank's senior preferred unsecured funding over €STR by tenor.

sections.heading: Counterparty reference data and credit curve mapping
sections.text: Counterparties are identified by LEI and the internal counterparty ID, trades by the Apex trade ID and the UTI, and netting agreements by the LegalHub agreement ID; these identifiers follow the Group naming conventions. Each counterparty is mapped either to its own liquid CDS curve (138 counterparties, 41% of CVA) or to a proxy curve determined by its internal rating, sector and region (1,314 counterparties, 59% of CVA); the mapping, the proxy attributes and the proxy curve are stored per counterparty. The internal rating is mapped to the seven rating buckets of the proxy regression through the Bank's master scale.

sections.heading: Exclusions
sections.text: The following trades are excluded from the XVA calculation, with number and share of the 38,400 OTC derivative trades: (a) centrally cleared trades with qualifying CCPs, 21,700 (56.5%), whose counterparty credit and funding exposure is covered by daily variation margin and default fund arrangements; (b) intragroup trades with consolidated subsidiaries, 1,160 (3.0%), eliminated at group level; and (c) trades with counterparties in default, 38 (0.1%), which receive a specific credit adjustment by Product Control. The impact analysis in section 5.3 concludes that the exclusions do not bias the XVA of the remaining portfolio, and the exclusion of defaulted counterparties is reflected in a specific adjustment of EUR 2.3 million outside the model. Exclusion (a) is consistent with market practice for the measurement of CVA and FVA; the margin valuation adjustment on initial margin posted to CCPs is outside the scope of the model.

sections.heading: Missing values and outliers
sections.text: Missing values are classified per variable as structural (for example no threshold in a CSA without threshold), missing at random (a market data point not delivered on a given day) or caused by a data deficiency (for example a CSA term not captured in LegalHub). Missing market data points are filled by the market data interpolation of the front-office curve construction, and missing CSA terms are set conservatively (zero threshold received, unlimited threshold posted); the share of values filled in this way is reported in Annex C (0.3% of market data points and 0.8% of CSA terms), and the effect of the conservative CSA defaults on CVA is quantified at +EUR 0.6 million. Outliers in CDS spreads are identified by a daily change larger than five times the 60-day median absolute change or a spread inversion across tenors, with the same criteria in development and production. Flagged spreads are verified against a broker quote; confirmed moves are retained and erroneous values replaced by the previous day's value with a spread shift from the sector index, and the quarterly impact on CVA is quantified (EUR 0.1 million in 2026).

sections.heading: Proxy curve data
sections.text: For counterparties without liquid CDS, credit spreads are proxied with a cross-sectional regression of log five-year CDS spreads of 1,108 liquid reference entities on rating, sector and region factors (7 rating buckets, 8 sectors, 4 regions), re-estimated monthly; the term structure of the proxy is taken from the iTraxx or CDX index curve of the corresponding rating class. The regression was validated out of sample by excluding 10% of the liquid names in each monthly estimation: over 2026 the median absolute error of the proxy spread against the observed five-year spread was 14% and the mean error −2%, within the thresholds of 25% and ±10% set in the monitoring plan.

sections.heading: Representativeness
sections.text: Appropriateness of the data is assessed as the representativeness of the liquid CDS universe for the counterparties whose spreads are proxied: 91% of proxied CVA falls in rating-sector-region cells with at least 15 liquid reference entities, while the remaining 9% (mainly sub-investment grade corporates in the Benelux) rely on neighbouring cells. The distribution of the proxied counterparties by rating is more concentrated in BBB and BB than the liquid universe, which is dominated by A and BBB names; the regression factor for BB is estimated from 96 liquid names. The back-testing sample is representative of the portfolio's risk factors: it covers the nine simulated currencies, 94% of the FX pairs by exposure and all rate tenors used by the trades. Detailed analyses are presented in Annex B.

sections.heading: Representativeness for other uses
sections.text: The same data and exposure engine produce the potential future exposure (PFE) used for counterparty credit limits, for which real-world rather than risk-neutral drifts are applied. For this secondary use, the representativeness of the three-year correlation window was confirmed by back-testing the 95% PFE on the 2019–2026 anchor dates, with 5.6% exceedances against the expected 5%. The data set is not used for the regulatory CVA risk own funds requirement, which is calculated with the basic approach (BA-CVA) from regulatory exposure data.

sections.heading: Impact of exclusions
sections.text: The impact of exclusion (a) was tested by including the cleared trades with their daily variation margin: the resulting CVA and FVA contributions are below EUR 0.05 million, confirming that the exclusion is immaterial. Intragroup trades (b) have no effect at group level. The exclusion of defaulted counterparties (c) removes EUR 4.1 million of receivables from the model scope, which are covered by specific adjustments of EUR 2.3 million; no exclusion exceeds 5% of the exposure of any segment, so no model owner approval under MRM-STD-022 §5.3 was required.

sections.heading: Data quality assessment
sections.text: Data quality is assessed on completeness, accuracy, consistency and timeliness, complemented by validity and uniqueness, in EVD-14-DQ of 5 February 2027. The assessment is performed on every new frozen data set used for recalibration and on the data used for each periodic validation. Of 112 rules on critical data elements, 108 are green, 4 amber and none red; the amber results concern CSA independent amount completeness, stale proxy override reasons, and two CDS curves with inverted spreads that were verified as genuine. The assessment concludes that the data are fit for their intended use; it was signed off by the model developer on 3 February 2027 and by the model owner on 5 February 2027, before the data set was frozen.

sections.heading: Data quality rules and thresholds
sections.text: For every critical data element at least one rule is defined for each applicable mandatory dimension, with the reason recorded where a dimension does not apply. The rules are documented in Annex A of EVD-14-DQ and the 86 recurring rules run daily in the Group DQ monitoring tool, both on the RDS and on the production input data of the XVA engine. Each rule has an amber and a red threshold at least as strict as the defaults of MRM-STD-022 §4.3: CSA terms completeness amber below 99.5% and red below 99%, collateral balance reconciliation amber above 0.5% and red above 1% of the balance, and market data timeliness amber after 20:00 CET and red after 22:00 CET on the valuation date. Each critical data element has a business definition, a technical definition and DQ rules per applicable dimension, referenced by rule identifier in the data dictionary.

sections.heading: Reconciliation and independent verification of inputs
sections.text: Trade populations are reconciled daily between Apex and the XVA engine by trade count and notional, and collateral balances monthly between CollatPro and the general ledger; in December 2026 all 16,700 trades reconciled and collateral balances differed by EUR 0.2 million (0.01%). The XVA figures are reconciled monthly with the general ledger postings and with the valuation adjustments reported in the FINREP templates. Market prices and model inputs, including CDS spreads, swaption volatilities and the funding curve, are verified at least monthly by Product Control, which is independent of the XVA desk and the other trading desks; differences above the IPV thresholds are adjusted in the books and reported to the Valuation Committee. The critical data elements are reconciled against source at least annually as part of the year-end reconciliation, and unexplained differences are recorded as data quality issues.

sections.heading: Personal data and fair treatment
sections.text: Not applicable. All counterparties in the scope of the model are legal entities, identified by LEI; FX forwards of private banking clients are booked in the systems of the private banking entity and are outside the scope of the model. The data set therefore contains no personal data, and no DPIA or screening for protected attributes is required. The Privacy Office confirmed this on 9 January 2026 (PRIV-2026-0112), and the inventory record states that no personal data is processed.

sections.heading: Reproducibility
sections.text: The RDS build code is held in repository bitbucket.bank.local/foqa/xva-rds-build; XVA-RDS-2026Q4-F1 was produced with tag xva-rds-v2.3.1 from the source snapshots of 31 December 2026 (Apex, LegalHub, CollatPro and MDR extracts of 4 January 2027, FTP curve of 31 December 2026). A full rebuild on 8 February 2027 reproduced the frozen data set exactly: 16,700 trades, 2,310 netting sets, 1,452 counterparties and 2,114,862 market data observations, with zero differences. The frozen data set is stored read-only under the version identifier XVA-RDS-2026Q4-F1 with its build code tag, lineage and metadata, and corrections are made only by issuing a new version with the original retained. Archived versions are retained for the life of the model and at least ten years after its decommissioning. This documentation and the data dictionary are intended to allow Model Validation to rebuild the data set independently from source data.

sections.heading: Choice of observation window
sections.text: The three-year window for correlations balances responsiveness and statistical stability; it contains the 2024 easing cycle and the market turbulence of April 2025, and correlations estimated over five years including the 2022 rate shock differ by less than 0.05 for the main pairs (sensitivity in EVD-14-MDD section 7.4). The two-year window for the proxy regression reflects the liquidity of the CDS market; a longer window would include reference entities whose liquidity has since changed. The back-testing window from 2019 covers the negative rate period, the COVID-19 turmoil, the 2022 rate shock and the 2023 banking stress. Volatilities and drifts are not estimated from history: the exposure model is calibrated risk-neutrally to market prices of the valuation date, consistently with the pricing of the trades.

sections.heading: Missing values and outliers
sections.text: Missing values are classified per variable as structural (for example no threshold in a CSA without threshold), missing at random (a market data point not delivered on a given day) or caused by a data deficiency (for example a CSA term not captured in LegalHub). Outliers in CDS spreads are identified by a daily change larger than five times the 60-day median absolute change or a spread inversion across tenors, with the same criteria in development and production. Flagged spreads are verified against a broker quote; confirmed moves are retained and erroneous values replaced by the previous day's value with a spread shift from the sector index, and the quarterly impact on CVA is quantified (EUR 0.1 million in 2026).

sections.heading: Proxy curve data

sections.heading: Purpose, scope and intended use
sections.text: The Derivatives Valuation and XVA model (MDL-14, model version 4.2) calculates the credit valuation adjustment (CVA), the debit valuation adjustment (DVA) and the funding valuation adjustment (FVA) of the Bank's bilateral OTC derivatives for the measurement of fair value under IFRS 13, and provides the exposure profiles and sensitivities used by the XVA desk to manage these adjustments. Secondary uses are the potential future exposure for counterparty credit limits and the inputs to the unearned credit spread, investing and funding cost and model risk additional valuation adjustments (AVAs) under Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2016/101, which are deducted from CET1 capital. At 31 December 2026 the model produced a CVA of EUR −48.7 million, a DVA of EUR +21.3 million and an FVA of EUR −17.9 million (funding cost adjustment −24.6 million, funding benefit adjustment +6.7 million) on 16,700 trades in 2,310 netting sets. The model is developed and owned by Front Office Quantitative Analytics and is managed under MRM-POL-001; it runs on the Bank's own XVA engine and uses no vendor model component.

sections.heading: Range of application and usage restrictions
sections.text: The model applies to bilateral OTC interest rate, FX and inflation derivatives of the Amsterdam head office and the London branch: interest rate swaps, cross-currency swaps, FX forwards and swaps, European FX options, European and Bermudan swaptions, caps and floors, and zero-coupon inflation swaps. The model limitations result in usage restrictions: exposures are simulated for nine currencies (EUR, USD, GBP, CHF, JPY, SEK, NOK, DKK and PLN) and maturities up to 50 years, FX options only up to ten years, and path-dependent exotic products (for example target redemption forwards) are outside the approved scope and receive an XVA from a conservative add-on approved by the Valuation Committee. Trades in other currencies (0.9% of expected exposure) are mapped to EUR with an FX volatility add-on. A new product that is not within the approved scope is not traded before the model is extended and approved or a temporary approval with trading limits is granted through the new product approval process.

sections.heading: Model structure and components
sections.text: The model consists of five components: (1) the scenario generator, which simulates interest rates, FX rates and inflation indices under the risk-neutral measure; (2) the trade pricers, which revalue every trade on every path and time step; (3) the collateral module, which applies netting and CSA terms to produce collateralised exposures; (4) the XVA integrator, which combines expected positive and negative exposures with credit and funding curves; and (5) the sensitivity module, which computes XVA sensitivities by bump and revalue for hedging. Fair value is measured as the exit price that would be received to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date; the XVAs adjust the risk-free, collateral-discounted front-office value of the trades to this exit price. The model runs daily for risk management and at each month end for the official fair value.

sections.heading: Dependencies on other models and systems
sections.text: The trade pricers in the XVA engine are the analytic and lattice pricers of the front-office pricing library FOPL 7.4, reused for consistency with the front-office valuation; Bermudan swaptions are priced on the simulated paths by least-squares Monte Carlo regression, which is benchmarked against the FOPL lattice price at time zero. The model depends on the curve construction of the Market Data Repository, on the internal ratings of the Credit Rating System for the proxy mapping, and on Treasury's funds transfer pricing curve. Downstream, the XVA figures are posted to the general ledger by Product Control and used in the prudent valuation calculation.

sections.heading: Alternatives considered and selection rationale
sections.text: At the redevelopment of version 4.0 and again for the annual review, four approaches were assessed against documented criteria (consistency with the front-office valuation, treatment of netting and collateral, accuracy for the portfolio's products, stability of the XVA and its sensitivities, run time for daily hedging and transparency): (a) Monte Carlo simulation with a one-factor Hull-White model per currency and lognormal FX; (b) Monte Carlo with a two-factor Gaussian (G2++) rates model; (c) a LIBOR market model simulation; and (d) a semi-analytic CVA per trade using swaption replication. Approach (a) was selected: it captures netting and collateral at portfolio level, which rules out (d); the two-factor model changes the expected exposure by less than 3% for 95% of the netting sets but doubles the run time and makes the daily sensitivities less stable; and the market model gives no material accuracy gain for a portfolio dominated by swaps and cross-currency swaps. The two-factor model is retained as an alternative model for the model risk AVA (section 4.8).

sections.heading: Fair value principles and valuation adjustments
sections.text: The XVAs reflect the assumptions that market participants would use in pricing the derivatives, assuming they act in their economic best interest: CVA and DVA use market-implied default probabilities and recovery rates, and FVA uses a funding spread representative of the funding costs of market participants active in the principal market rather than an entity-specific cost. The fair value of derivative liabilities reflects non-performance risk, including the Bank's own credit risk, through the DVA calculated with the Bank's five-year senior CDS spread (52 basis points at 31 December 2026). Under the portfolio exception of IFRS 13 paragraph 48, the Bank measures the credit adjustments on the net exposure per counterparty, because the portfolio is managed on that basis under the documented counterparty risk management strategy and reported to key management personnel on that basis in the monthly XVA report to the Valuation Committee. The DVA is excluded from CET1 capital under Article 33(1)(c) CRR, and the difference between the accounting fair value and the prudent value is covered by the AVAs described in section 4.8.

sections.heading: Exposure simulation
sections.text: The exposure simulation uses 5,000 Sobol paths with Brownian bridge construction on 128 time steps (daily for two weeks, weekly to three months, monthly to two years, quarterly to ten years and semi-annually to 50 years), with the risk-neutral calibration of section 5, consistent with the pricing of the trades. Expected positive exposure EPE(t) and expected negative exposure ENE(t) are computed per netting set as the path averages of the positive and negative parts of the collateralised netting set value. The valuation technique is appropriate in the circumstances because the portfolio's XVA depends on the joint evolution of rates, FX and collateral over the life of the trades; the simulation maximises the use of observable inputs by calibrating to quoted swaptions, FX options and inflation swaps and minimises unobservable inputs, which are limited to correlations, long-dated volatilities and proxy spreads. The simulation error of the CVA, measured by the standard error over 20 independent seeds, is 0.4% at portfolio level and below 2% for 97% of the netting sets.

sections.heading: Interest rate model
sections.text: Interest rates in each currency follow a one-factor Hull-White model on the €STR, SOFR, SONIA and other risk-free rate discount curves, with deterministic tenor basis spreads to the projection curves (EURIBOR 3M and 6M) and deterministic cross-currency basis. The volatility is piecewise constant and calibrated daily to the co-terminal ATM swaptions of each currency, and the mean reversion is fixed at 0.03 for all currencies (EJ-14-01); the model reprices the calibration swaptions with a root mean square error of 0.62 basis points of normal volatility on average in 2026 for EUR. Negative rates are allowed by the Gaussian dynamics, which is consistent with the Bachelier quotation of the calibration instruments. The deterministic basis spreads are a known limitation (L-14-03), covered by a model reserve.

sections.heading: FX, inflation and correlations
sections.text: FX rates against EUR follow lognormal processes with time-dependent volatilities calibrated to ATM FX options up to ten years and extrapolated flat beyond; the drift is determined by the simulated interest rate differentials, so that forward FX rates are reproduced. EUR and US inflation indices are simulated with a one-factor model for the real rate following the Jarrow-Yildirim approach, calibrated to zero-coupon inflation swaps and to the volatility implied by year-on-year inflation caps where quoted. Correlations between the risk factors are estimated from 156 weekly returns over three years because implied correlations are not observable for most pairs; the use of historical correlations in an otherwise risk-neutral calibration is a documented assumption (A-14-03) and its effect is included in the model risk AVA. The correlation matrix is recalibrated quarterly and made positive definite by the nearest-correlation-matrix algorithm with a maximum adjustment of 0.02.

sections.heading: Netting and collateral modelling
sections.text: Exposures are aggregated per netting set only where the ISDA master agreement is covered by a positive legal netting opinion, and the CVA reflects the net credit exposure after netting and collateral arrangements that market participants would take into account, including their expected legal enforceability. For netting sets with a CSA the collateral balance at each time step is modelled from the threshold, minimum transfer amount and independent amount, with a margin period of risk of 10 business days between the last successful margin call and the close-out, during which the exposure evolves without collateral adjustment. Collateral in currencies other than the CSA base currency is converted at the simulated FX rates, and non-cash collateral is valued with the haircuts of the CSA. At 31 December 2026, 1,380 of the 2,310 netting sets have a CSA with daily variation margin; they account for 71% of the gross positive fair value but only 18% of the CVA.

sections.heading: Wrong-way risk
sections.text: Specific wrong-way risk, where the exposure is legally or economically connected to the counterparty (for example cross-currency swaps with sovereign issuers in their own currency, or trades referencing the counterparty's own shares or debt), is identified at trade inception and at each month end; the 14 affected netting sets are valued with a jump-to-default adjustment that assumes an FX devaluation or loss of the reference asset at default. General wrong-way risk from the correlation between counterparty credit quality and market risk factors is not modelled in the simulation, which assumes independence between default times and market risk factors. The effect of general wrong-way risk was estimated with a credit-FX and credit-rates correlation stress for the 25 largest uncollateralised netting sets and is covered by a model reserve of EUR 2.1 million (section 4.9 and limitation L-14-01).

sections.heading: CVA and DVA
sections.text: Unilateral CVA and DVA are calculated per netting set as CVA = −LGD(c) × Σ EPE(t(i)) × DF(t(i)) × [S(c, t(i−1)) − S(c, t(i))] and DVA = −LGD(B) × Σ ENE(t(i)) × DF(t(i)) × [S(B, t(i−1)) − S(B, t(i))], where S denotes the survival probability implied by the counterparty's or the Bank's credit curve and DF the collateral discount factor. First-to-default effects are ignored, which is the prevailing market practice for accounting CVA and is conservative for the net CVA-DVA position of the Bank. LGDs are market-implied: the recovery rate quoted with the counterparty's CDS where available and 40% for senior unsecured claims otherwise. The XVAs are allocated to trades by the Euler allocation of the expected exposure for the P&L attribution of the desks.

sections.heading: Counterparty credit curves and proxies
sections.text: CVA uses market-implied default probabilities bootstrapped from the counterparty's own CDS curve where a liquid CDS exists (138 counterparties with at least three contributors per day on 80% of business days) and otherwise from a proxy curve. The proxy methodology, introduced with version 4.2 and documented in EVD-14-RDS section 4.4, is a monthly cross-sectional regression of log five-year CDS spreads of 1,108 liquid reference entities on rating, sector and region factors, with the term structure of the relevant credit index; it was validated in the change validation of October 2026 and is tested out of sample every month (median absolute error 14% in 2026). Proxy spreads are floored at the spread of the counterparty's sovereign of domicile for corporates and financials, to avoid proxies below the sovereign ceiling. Where bonds of the counterparty trade with observable spreads, the proxy is compared with the bond-implied spread in the monthly IPV, and deviations above 50% are escalated to the Valuation Committee.

sections.heading: FVA and the DVA–FVA overlap
sections.text: FVA reflects the cost and benefit of funding uncollateralised and partially collateralised exposures: the funding cost adjustment applies the Bank's funding spread over €STR (64 basis points at five years at 31 December 2026) to the EPE, and the funding benefit adjustment applies only the liquidity component of the funding spread not already reflected in DVA (12 basis points at five years) to the ENE, so that own credit is not counted twice. The funding curve and the treatment of the DVA–FVA overlap were approved by the Valuation Committee on 18 November 2025 (decision VC-2025-11-03) and reconfirmed on 12 January 2027. FVA is included in the fair value because market participants in the principal market for uncollateralised derivatives, the Bank's dealer peers, include funding costs and benefits in pricing at the measurement date, as evidenced by the Bank's analysis of 23 novation and unwind transactions in 2026, in which the traded prices implied an FVA within 15% of the model FVA.

sections.heading: Fair value hierarchy and day-one profit
sections.text: Each fair value measurement is categorised in its entirety at the level of the lowest-level input that is significant to the entire measurement: a netting set is Level 3 when an unobservable input (a proxy spread for a counterparty rated below investment grade, a correlation or a long-dated volatility) changes its fair value by more than 10% under a reasonably possible alternative. Where an observable input is adjusted with an unobservable input that significantly changes fair value, as the CVA with a proxy spread for a sub-investment grade counterparty, the measurement is Level 3; at 31 December 2026 Level 3 derivative assets amounted to EUR 214 million and liabilities to EUR 97 million. Day-one profit on trades with significant unobservable inputs is deferred in accordance with the accounting policy and released over the life of the trade or when the inputs become observable; the deferred balance was EUR 3.2 million at 31 December 2026. The Level 3 measurements include a risk adjustment for model and input uncertainty where market participants would include one, through the model reserves of section 4.9.

sections.heading: Calibration of the Hull-White model
sections.text: The volatility of each currency is calibrated daily to the co-terminal ATM swaptions with final maturity 30 years (20 years for currencies other than EUR, USD and GBP); calibration errors are monitored daily against thresholds (normal volatility RMSE amber above 1.5 basis points, red above 3.0 basis points), and breaches are escalated to the Head of Front Office Quantitative Analytics and Product Control the same day. In 2026 the EUR calibration was amber on 7 days and never red; the amber days coincided with the extreme swaption moves of April 2025 and March 2026 and were resolved by recalibration with an extended instrument set. The appropriateness of the calibration inputs and parameters is assessed monthly in the model performance report, including the stability of the calibrated volatilities over time.

sections.heading: Calibration to the transaction price

sections.heading: Exposure model back-testing
sections.text: The simulated risk factor distributions are back-tested on 96 monthly anchor dates from 2019 to 2026 at horizons of one week, one month, three months, six months and one year, using the probability integral transform of the realised moves and the Anderson-Darling test; 94% of the 170 risk factor-horizon combinations are green (p-value above 5%) and 6% amber, all at the one-year horizon for EUR rates during the 2022 rate shock. Results are reported per currency and per product-type portfolio, which are the material segments of the model. The amber results at the one-year horizon were analysed: they reflect the risk-neutral calibration, which does not anticipate the 2022 regime change, recorded as limitation L-14-04 and mitigated by the market price uncertainty AVA.

sections.heading: Calibration quality and P&L explain
sections.text: The calibration errors of section 5.1 were within threshold on 98% of business days in 2026 across all currencies. The comparison of close-out values of 23 novations and unwinds in 2026 with the model XVA showed differences within ±15%, which supports the accuracy of the model.

sections.heading: Benchmarking
sections.text: The model is compared with the two-factor rates model as challenger: the expected exposure differs by less than 3% for 95% of the netting sets, and the CVA by 1.9% at portfolio level; the differences are explained by the decorrelation of long and short rates, which matters mainly for Bermudan swaptions. sections.heading: Production controls and change control
sections.text: Code is held in the Bank's version control system and each production version is tagged (xva-engine-v4.2.0) and retrievable; changes follow change management with four-eyes review by a person other than the author and documented approval before deployment. A secure copy of each production version is held in the release archive, and Product Control uses it quarterly to recompute the XVA of a sample of 50 netting sets independently of the production run. sections.heading: Purpose, scope and intended use
sections.text: The Derivatives Valuation and XVA model (MDL-14, model version 4.2) calculates the credit valuation adjustment (CVA), the debit valuation adjustment (DVA) and the funding valuation adjustment (FVA) of the Bank's bilateral OTC derivatives for the measurement of fair value under IFRS 13, and provides the exposure profiles and sensitivities used by the XVA desk to manage these adjustments. Secondary uses are the potential future exposure for counterparty credit limits and the inputs to the unearned credit spread, investing and funding cost and model risk additional valuation adjustments (AVAs) under Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2016/101, which are deducted from CET1 capital. At 31 December 2026 the model produced a CVA of EUR −48.7 million, a DVA of EUR +21.3 million and an FVA of EUR −17.9 million (funding cost adjustment −24.6 million, funding benefit adjustment +6.7 million) on 16,700 trades in 2,310 netting sets. The model is developed and owned by Front Office Quantitative Analytics and is managed under MRM-POL-001; it runs on the Bank's own XVA engine and uses no vendor model component.

sections.heading: Range of application and usage restrictions
sections.text: The model applies to bilateral OTC interest rate, FX and inflation derivatives of the Amsterdam head office and the London branch: interest rate swaps, cross-currency swaps, FX forwards and swaps, European FX options, European and Bermudan swaptions, caps and floors, and zero-coupon inflation swaps. The model limitations result in usage restrictions: exposures are simulated for nine currencies (EUR, USD, GBP, CHF, JPY, SEK, NOK, DKK and PLN) and maturities up to 50 years, FX options only up to ten years, and path-dependent exotic products (for example target redemption forwards) are outside the approved scope and receive an XVA from a conservative add-on approved by the Valuation Committee. Trades in other currencies (0.9% of expected exposure) are mapped to EUR with an FX volatility add-on. A new product that is not within the approved scope is not traded before the model is extended and approved or a temporary approval with trading limits is granted through the new product approval process.

sections.heading: Model structure and components
sections.text: The model consists of five components: (1) the scenario generator, which simulates interest rates, FX rates and inflation indices under the risk-neutral measure; (2) the trade pricers, which revalue every trade on every path and time step; (3) the collateral module, which applies netting and CSA terms to produce collateralised exposures; (4) the XVA integrator, which combines expected positive and negative exposures with credit and funding curves; and (5) the sensitivity module, which computes XVA sensitivities by bump and revalue for hedging. Fair value is measured as the exit price that would be received to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date; the XVAs adjust the risk-free, collateral-discounted front-office value of the trades to this exit price. The model runs daily for risk management and at each month end for the official fair value.

sections.heading: Dependencies on other models and systems

sections.heading: Alternatives considered and selection rationale
sections.text: At the redevelopment of version 4.0 and again for the annual review, four approaches were assessed against documented criteria (consistency with the front-office valuation, treatment of netting and collateral, accuracy for the portfolio's products, stability of the XVA and its sensitivities, run time for daily hedging and transparency): (a) Monte Carlo simulation with a one-factor Hull-White model per currency and lognormal FX; (b) Monte Carlo with a two-factor Gaussian (G2++) rates model; (c) a LIBOR market model simulation; and (d) a semi-analytic CVA per trade using swaption replication. Approach (a) was selected: it captures netting and collateral at portfolio level, which rules out (d); the two-factor model changes the expected exposure by less than 3% for 95% of the netting sets but doubles the run time and makes the daily sensitivities less stable; and the market model gives no material accuracy gain for a portfolio dominated by swaps and cross-currency swaps. The two-factor model is retained as an alternative model for the model risk AVA (section 4.8).

sections.heading: Fair value principles and valuation adjustments
sections.text: The XVAs reflect the assumptions that market participants would use in pricing the derivatives, assuming they act in their economic best interest: CVA and DVA use market-implied default probabilities and recovery rates, and FVA uses a funding spread representative of the funding costs of market participants active in the principal market rather than an entity-specific cost. The fair value of derivative liabilities reflects non-performance risk, including the Bank's own credit risk, through the DVA calculated with the Bank's five-year senior CDS spread (52 basis points at 31 December 2026). Under the portfolio exception of IFRS 13 paragraph 48, the Bank measures the credit adjustments on the net exposure per counterparty, because the portfolio is managed on that basis under the documented counterparty risk management strategy and reported to key management personnel on that basis in the monthly XVA report to the Valuation Committee. The DVA is excluded from CET1 capital under Article 33(1)(c) CRR, and the difference between the accounting fair value and the prudent value is covered by the AVAs described in section 4.8.

sections.heading: Exposure simulation
sections.text: The exposure simulation uses 5,000 Sobol paths with Brownian bridge construction on 128 time steps (daily for two weeks, weekly to three months, monthly to two years, quarterly to ten years and semi-annually to 50 years), with the risk-neutral calibration of section 5, consistent with the pricing of the trades. Expected positive exposure EPE(t) and expected negative exposure ENE(t) are computed per netting set as the path averages of the positive and negative parts of the collateralised netting set value. The valuation technique is appropriate in the circumstances because the portfolio's XVA depends on the joint evolution of rates, FX and collateral over the life of the trades; the simulation maximises the use of observable inputs by calibrating to quoted swaptions, FX options and inflation swaps and minimises unobservable inputs, which are limited to correlations, long-dated volatilities and proxy spreads. The simulation error of the CVA, measured by the standard error over 20 independent seeds, is 0.4% at portfolio level and below 2% for 97% of the netting sets.

sections.heading: Interest rate model
sections.text: Interest rates in each currency follow a one-factor Hull-White model on the €STR, SOFR, SONIA and other risk-free rate discount curves, with deterministic tenor basis spreads to the projection curves (EURIBOR 3M and 6M) and deterministic cross-currency basis. The volatility is piecewise constant and calibrated daily to the co-terminal ATM swaptions of each currency, and the mean reversion is fixed at 0.03 for all currencies (EJ-14-01); the model reprices the calibration swaptions with a root mean square error of 0.62 basis points of normal volatility on average in 2026 for EUR. Negative rates are allowed by the Gaussian dynamics, which is consistent with the Bachelier quotation of the calibration instruments. The deterministic basis spreads are a known limitation (L-14-03), covered by a model reserve.

sections.heading: FX, inflation and correlations
sections.text: FX rates against EUR follow lognormal processes with time-dependent volatilities calibrated to ATM FX options up to ten years and extrapolated flat beyond; the drift is determined by the simulated interest rate differentials, so that forward FX rates are reproduced. Correlations between the risk factors are estimated from 156 weekly returns over three years because implied correlations are not observable for most pairs; the use of historical correlations in an otherwise risk-neutral calibration is a documented assumption (A-14-03) and its effect is included in the model risk AVA. The correlation matrix is recalibrated quarterly and made positive definite by the nearest-correlation-matrix algorithm with a maximum adjustment of 0.02.

sections.heading: Netting and collateral modelling
sections.text: Exposures are aggregated per netting set only where the ISDA master agreement is covered by a positive legal netting opinion, and the CVA reflects the net credit exposure after netting and collateral arrangements that market participants would take into account, including their expected legal enforceability. For netting sets with a CSA the collateral balance at each time step is modelled from the threshold, minimum transfer amount and independent amount, with a margin period of risk of 10 business days between the last successful margin call and the close-out, during which the exposure evolves without collateral adjustment. Collateral in currencies other than the CSA base currency is converted at the simulated FX rates, and non-cash collateral is valued with the haircuts of the CSA. At 31 December 2026, 1,380 of the 2,310 netting sets have a CSA with daily variation margin; they account for 71% of the gross positive fair value but only 18% of the CVA.

sections.heading: Wrong-way risk
sections.text: Specific wrong-way risk, where the exposure is legally or economically connected to the counterparty (for example cross-currency swaps with sovereign issuers in their own currency, or trades referencing the counterparty's own shares or debt), is identified at trade inception and at each month end; the 14 affected netting sets are valued with a jump-to-default adjustment that assumes an FX devaluation or loss of the reference asset at default. sections.heading: CVA and DVA
sections.text: Unilateral CVA and DVA are calculated per netting set as CVA = −LGD(c) × Σ EPE(t(i)) × DF(t(i)) × [S(c, t(i−1)) − S(c, t(i))] and DVA = −LGD(B) × Σ ENE(t(i)) × DF(t(i)) × [S(B, t(i−1)) − S(B, t(i))], where S denotes the survival probability implied by the counterparty's or the Bank's credit curve and DF the collateral discount factor. First-to-default effects are ignored, which is the prevailing market practice for accounting CVA and is conservative for the net CVA-DVA position of the Bank. LGDs are market-implied: the recovery rate quoted with the counterparty's CDS where available and 40% for senior unsecured claims otherwise. The XVAs are allocated to trades by the Euler allocation of the expected exposure for the P&L attribution of the desks.

sections.heading: Counterparty credit curves and proxies
sections.text: CVA uses market-implied default probabilities bootstrapped from the counterparty's own CDS curve where a liquid CDS exists (138 counterparties with at least three contributors per day on 80% of business days) and otherwise from a proxy curve. The proxy methodology, introduced with version 4.2 and documented in EVD-14-RDS section 4.4, is a monthly cross-sectional regression of log five-year CDS spreads of 1,108 liquid reference entities on rating, sector and region factors, with the term structure of the relevant credit index; it was validated in the change validation of October 2026 and is tested out of sample every month (median absolute error 14% in 2026). Proxy spreads are floored at the spread of the counterparty's sovereign of domicile for corporates and financials, to avoid proxies below the sovereign ceiling. Where bonds of the counterparty trade with observable spreads, the proxy is compared with the bond-implied spread in the monthly IPV, and deviations above 50% are escalated to the Valuation Committee.

sections.heading: FVA and the DVA–FVA overlap

The funding curve and the treatment of the DVA–FVA overlap were approved by the Valuation Committee on 18 November 2025 (decision VC-2025-11-03) and reconfirmed on 12 January 2027. FVA is included in the fair value because market participants in the principal market for uncollateralised derivatives, the Bank's dealer peers, include funding costs and benefits in pricing at the measurement date, as evidenced by the Bank's analysis of 23 novation and unwind transactions in 2026, in which the traded prices implied an FVA within 15% of the model FVA.

sections.text: The simulated risk factor distributions are back-tested on 96 monthly anchor dates from 2019 to 2026 at horizons of one week, one month, three months, six months and one year, using the probability integral transform of the realised moves and the Anderson-Darling test; 94% of the 170 risk factor-horizon combinations are green (p-value above 5%) and 6% amber, all at the one-year horizon for EUR rates during the 2022 rate shock. Results are reported per currency and per product-type portfolio, which are the material segments of the model. The amber results at the one-year horizon were analysed: they reflect the risk-neutral calibration, which does not anticipate the 2022 regime change, recorded as limitation L-14-04 and mitigated by the market price uncertainty AVA.

sections.heading: Sensitivity analysis

The expert judgement on the mean reversion (EJ-14-01) and on the proxy factors (EJ-14-03) was tested under reasonable alternatives with these results. sections.heading: Material assumptions

A-14-01 is supported by the benchmarking against the two-factor model, A-14-02 by market practice and IFRS 13, and A-14-03 and A-14-04 by the model reserves and the model risk AVA. sections.text: The monitoring plan, approved by the model owner on 12 February 2027 and reviewed by Model Validation, defines the KPIs with calculation, amber and red thresholds, frequency, data, segments, responsible persons and escalation per traffic light. KPIs are computed at portfolio level and per currency or product type. The monitoring report is produced semi-annually, the minimum for Tier 2 models, and finalised within 60 calendar days after the end of the period. Thresholds based on observed market data (calibration errors, proxy errors against observed CDS spreads and IPV differences) determine when the model is no longer sufficiently robust and must be recalibrated or redeveloped.

deficiencies.rationale: The MDD and RDS documentation describe the regression proxy methodology, its monthly out-of-sample test (median absolute error 14%) and its validation at the version 4.2 change, which on the documentation looks adequate. Model Validation compared the proxy spreads of the 86 sub-investment grade financial counterparties with the spreads implied by their traded senior bonds and found the proxies on average 35% below the bond-implied level; the out-of-sample test cannot detect this because the liquid CDS universe contains only nine sub-investment grade financials. The CVA of these counterparties is understated by an estimated EUR 2.7 million.

mitigation.text: Add a bond-implied spread calibration for rating-sector cells with fewer than 15 liquid CDS names, or a conservative cell-level add-on, and extend the out-of-sample test to bond-implied spreads. Until then, book a model reserve of EUR 2.7 million approved by the Valuation Committee.

deficiencies.rationale: Specific wrong-way risk is identified and valued with a jump-to-default adjustment, but general wrong-way risk is not captured in the exposure simulation; it is covered only by a model reserve estimated with a correlation stress on the 25 largest uncollateralised netting sets, without evidence that the remaining netting sets are immaterial.

mitigation.text: Extend the general wrong-way risk assessment to all uncollateralised netting sets with material exposure and document the materiality conclusion, as required by the Model Approval Panel condition due 30 June 2027.

deficiencies.rationale: The prudence of the expert-based model risk AVA was confirmed against the alternative-models method for only two of the nine exotic valuation models in 2026, which is not a material sample of the models to which the expert-based approach is applied.

mitigation.text: Define a sample covering the majority of the expert-based model risk AVA and perform the annual confirmation against alternative models for that sample in the 2027 AVA review.

deficiencies.rationale: The monitoring plan defines valuation-specific KPIs, but the thresholds of the exposure back-testing KPI (amber below 90%, red below 80% green combinations) were set by the model owner and are not evidenced as approved by Model Risk Management.

mitigation.text: Submit the valuation KPI thresholds to Model Risk Management for approval and record the approval in the monitoring plan.
